tasks.registered_metrics_text:
a) Define the metric(s) to assess a property of an algorithm. These metrics should reflect the desired algorithm
properties described in assessment aim(s) (see above). State which metric(s) were used to compute the ranking(s) (if
any).
  • Example 1: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC)
  • Example 2: Area under curve (AUC)
Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC): for the segmentation of the four target regions (RNFL, GCC, other retinal layers
and choroid layer), the results are compared with the reference standards using the Dice Similarity Coefficient for
the four targets respectively.


Average unsigned surface detection error (AUSDE)[15]: to verify the accuracy of the boundaries of the
segmentation mask, we measure the absolute Euclidean distance in the y-axis between the predicted boundary
detection results and the reference standard.


Average signed surface detection error (ASSDE)[15]: to verify the accuracy of the boundaries of the segmentation
mask, we also measure the distance in the y-axis between the predicted boundary detection results and the
reference standard.

b) Justify why the metric(s) was/were chosen, preferably with reference to the biomedical application.

Dice Similarity Coefficient is usually used in medical segmentation evaluation.
AUSDE and ASSDE are used in the surface or boundary detection, and the unsigned errors provide a measure of
the overall amount of error without regard to the sign of error. In this challenge, we use both unsigned and signed
error to describe the performance of the algorithms.

tasks.registered_ranking_text:
a) Describe the method used to compute a performance rank for all submitted algorithms based on the generated
metric results on the test cases. Typically the text will describe how results obtained per case and metric are aggregated
to arrive at a final score/ranking.

For the four target segmentation results, we will calculate the DSC metrics (DSC_RNFL, DSC_GCIPL, DSC_other,
DSC_choroid), and then weighted combine these DSC metrics by: DSC_total =
0.3*DSC_RNFL+0.3*DSC_GCC+0.2DSC_other+0.2*DSC_choroid.


For the boundaries results obtained from the segmentation masks, we will respectively calculate the AUSDE and
ASSDE on the five boundaries, and then respectively equally combine these errors by: AUSDE_total =
0.2*AUSDE_RNFL+0.2*AUSDE_RNFL-GCIPL+0.2*AUSDE_GCIPL-other+0.2*AUSDE_other-
choroid+0.2*AUSDE_choroid;


ASSDE_total = 0.2*ASSDE_RNFL+0.2*ASSDE_RNFL-GCIPL+0.2*ASSDE_GCIPL-other+0.2*ASSDE_other-
choroid+0.2*ASSDE_choroid.


Each team receives a rank (1=best) for each metric based on the mean value of the measure over the set of test
data (R_DSC, R_AUSDE, R_ASSDE). The total ranking of this task is then determined by combining these three
individual ranks: R_task1 = 0.2*R_DSC+0.4*R_AUSDE+0.4*ASSDE.
The team with the lowest R_task1 will be ranked #1 on the task leaderboard.


In the challenge, the online and onsite competitions will have different weights for the final ranking, as:
Final ranking = 0.3 * online ranking + 0.7 * onsite ranking, where a higher weight is assigned to the results on the
test set.

b) Describe the method(s) used to manage submissions with missing results on test cases.

missing result will report an error information.

c) Justify why the described ranking scheme(s) was/were used.

In the DSC_total, we set the DSC_RNFL and DSC_GCIPL weights of 0.3 due that they are more important in the
diagnosis of glaucoma than other retinal and choroid layers.
In the final ranking formula R_task1, the ranking of AUSDE and AUSSDE are set higher weights to encourage the
participants to obtain the segmentation results with more accurate boundaries.


And, in the final ranking, we set the online weight of 0.3 to encourage the participants to obtain the staged result.
And to be fair to all participants, we set the onsite weight of 0.7 to guarantee the final ranking prefer on the onsite
test set. That’s because the teams can adjust their models after seeing the performance on the online dataset
through the leaderboard during the preliminary, while they cannot see the onsite dataset. Hence, compared with
the predicted results on the online dataset, those on the onsite dataset can reflect the real performance of the
models.

registered_task_submissions.protocol_description: The segmentation results in the OCT images should be provided in a “segmentation_results” folder, as one image per test image, with the segmented pixels labeled in the same way as in the reference standard (8-bit bmp files with 0: RFNL, 60: GCIPL, 120: Other structures of the retina, 180: Choroid, and 255: Elsewhere.) Meanwhile, the submitted segmentation files are requested to name according to the original image names and with the same extension.

The classification results should be provided in a single CSV file, named “classification_results.csv”, with the first column corresponding to the ID of the test data, and the second column containing the predicted classification results (0 or 1) for the glaucoma category.
